cases.learnTitle: Ischemic stroke on diffusion MRI (expert-approved lesion mask)
cases.contextSource: Dataset description (ISLES 2022: MRI of acute to subacute ischemic stroke).
cases.referenceSummary: The ischemic lesion was outlined with a model's help, corrected by trained annotators and a neuroradiologist in training, and approved by an attending neuroradiologist (ISLES 2022). The images are skull-stripped and resliced to 2 mm by the dataset authors; time since onset is not given.
cases.learnNotes: In an acute ischemic stroke the cells swell (cytotoxic edema) within minutes, which restricts the motion of water. Diffusion-weighted MRI shows this early as a bright area in an arterial territory, long before CT changes; the ADC map confirms true restriction when the same area is dark. Bright on DWI but not dark on ADC is 'T2 shine-through', not restriction. Name the territory (anterior, middle or posterior cerebral artery, or a watershed or lacunar pattern) and look for hemorrhage on the other sequences.

tasks.title: Find the restricted diffusion
tasks.prompt: Read the diffusion-weighted images from the skull base to the vertex. Mark the abnormal area (point or box), or state that you find none.

hints.text: Look for a bright area on DWI that keeps to an arterial territory, and compare the two hemispheres.
Jumping to a slice with the reference.

tasks.title: Is it true restriction?
tasks.prompt: Find the bright lesion on DWI, then look at the same place on the ADC map. How does it look on ADC?

options.why: Water motion is restricted in the swollen cells of an acute infarct, so the ADC is low and the map is dark.
A bright ADC means water moves more freely (e.g. CSF or old tissue loss), the opposite of restriction.
Then the DWI brightness would be T2 shine-through rather than restriction.

hints.text: Use the linked views: double-click the lesion on DWI and the ADC view goes to the same place.
